title: Cloudflare's pay-per-crawl isn't a new anti-scraping weapon, according to the team at ScrapingAnt. It's a payment rail: a site returns a 402
text:
Cloudflare's pay-per-crawl isn't a new anti-scraping weapon, according to the team at ScrapingAnt. It's a payment rail: a site returns a 402, a verified crawler signs its request with Web Bot Auth, and Stripe settles the payment. That's commerce, not defense, and it means a chunk of the web is quietly splitting into two economies: licensed and metered on one side, the open long tail on the other, with anti bot systems caught in between that still can't tell a legitimate agent from a bad bot.

Here's what stands out to me: that access layer is only half the problem. Getting past the gate, paid or not, doesn't make extraction cheap. Most agent pipelines still burn tokens asking a model to guess a CSS selector, then burn more tokens again next week when the page changes and the guess goes stale. That's the actual cost center hiding behind every scraping bill, separate from whatever a site charges at the door.

DeepScrape treats that as the real problem to solve. Selectors get generated once with an LLM, then reused deterministically and self heal when a page's structure changes, so the model only gets called again when something actually breaks, not on every single pass. The MCP server exposes those scrapers directly as tools inside Claude or Cursor, and Site to MCP turns any website into a structured source an agent can query on its own. Pay for access where a rail exists. Don't keep paying a model to re-read the same page a thousand times after that.

title: A single scraping operator running 80K IPs across 43 countries is exposed as a coordinated bot cluster hiding behind fabricated geolocation,
text:
A single scraping operator running 80K IPs across 43 countries is exposed as a coordinated bot cluster hiding behind fabricated geolocation, spoofed mobile identities, and a deliberately fragmented IP portfolio designed to defeat traditional blocklisting.

Key findings:

- CrowdSec's alpha bot detection feature, shipped in v1.8.0, surfaced the cluster dubbed "PaperPhone" within two weeks of community deployment. 75,000 IPs spread across 230 IP blocks and 80 networks are involved. The infrastructure predates discovery, with IPs progressively joining as more sensors came online and IP rotation accelerating as banned addresses cycled out. The full breadth only became visible because the detection layer shifted from "what is this IP doing" to "what is the client behind this IP actually running", a meaningful investigative pivot.

- Geographic diversity is manufactured, not real. Traffic claims to originate from 43 countries, but request timing betrays a single operator timezone. Japan 🇯🇵 peaks at 05:00 local with 18.7% night-share, India 🇮🇳 peaks at 01:00 with 18.5%. Synchronization across regions 13 to 14 hours apart (Japan 🇯🇵/US, Australia 🇦🇺/Canada) collapses when viewed in UTC, exposing a single coordinated pulse. IP blocks reinforce this: adjacent /23s in the same /22 are artificially geolocated to Brussels, Bangkok, Tokyo, and Paris, a deliberate fragmentation pattern repeated across all 230 blocks. WHOIS inconsistencies compound it, with ranges showing mismatched RIRs, registrant countries, and claimed geolocations simultaneously.

- Bot fingerprinting uncovered consistent lies at the browser layer. The cluster cycles through exactly 13 device identities: 5 Android variants (Pixel 9, Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra, others) and 7 iOS variants. Every single bot, regardless of claimed device, reported a 375x812 viewport matching iPhone 10/11 only, and every browser returned Google SwiftShader as the WebGL renderer via UNMASKED_RENDERER_WEBGL. SwiftShader is a CPU-based software renderer used when no GPU is available. Modern flagship Android hardware essentially never triggers it, and iOS devices run WebKit, making a SwiftShader signal on claimed iOS 14/15 technically impossible.

- M247 does not own the IP blocks but routes more than 20% of PaperPhone's traffic as transit provider. A small number of controlling entities own the majority of the 230 blocks, with ranges showing inter-regional transfers as recently as 2025 to obscure lineage. Block utilization density shows most ranges were used at or near full capacity during scraping operations, ruling out coincidental residential overlap and confirming this is purpose-built datacenter infrastructure dressed up as organic global traffic.

Practitioner takeaway: geoblocking fails against operators who manufacture geographic identity at the IP registration layer. The detection surface that actually works here is client-side behavioral fingerprinting: viewport dimensions, WebGL renderer strings, and timezone-to-request-time correlation. For threat hunters, UNMASKED_RENDERER_WEBGL returning SwiftShader on claimed mobile user agents is a high-confidence bot signal worth building into WAF and SIEM detection logic. When investigating scraping clusters, cross-reference AS ownership graphs against transit providers, not just WHOIS registrant country, because M247 routing 20% of traffic without owning a single block shows how transit-layer attribution matters. Full cluster data and IOC context are in the CrowdSec report.

title: Cloudflare no longer sells keeping bots out. It sells charging them.  That is the whole answer and it happened in the open. In 2025 Cloudfla
text:
Cloudflare no longer sells keeping bots out. It sells charging them.

That is the whole answer and it happened in the open. In 2025 Cloudflare began blocking AI crawlers by default and launched pay-per-crawl, letting publishers set a price for each request from an AI company rather than simply refusing it.

Blocking was the old product. The current product is a toll booth.

Which is why declared AI user agents get through where anonymous scrapers do not. A crawler that identifies itself can be metered, billed and attributed.

One that hides cannot.

Honest identification became the fast lane specifically because it is the billable lane.

Spoofing a user agent to get through is trivial and it always has been, because user agent is a self-reported string with no verification. That is a known weakness and it is why the serious version of this uses signed requests and cryptographic bot verification instead.

The mitigation exists. Most sites have not turned it on.

The irony in the post is real and it is pointed at the wrong layer. A network that started as a shield now sits between publishers and the companies training on them, taking a position in the middle of both.

Every infrastructure company eventually discovers that the toll is worth more than the wall.

The bots got in because somebody found a way to invoice them.

title: By one new count, 31.1% of web text in August 2026 was written by AI.  That number comes from a paper published this week. The team didn't s
text:
By one new count, 31.1% of web text in August 2026 was written by AI.

That number comes from a paper published this week. The team didn't stop at counting. They trained 800 language models on different mixes of human and AI-written web text and measured what happened.

The short version: AI text can help a little, then its value flips.

Train on the web as it is today, and you need 1.6× the compute to match a model trained only on the human part.

The strangest finding: repeating the same human text beat adding fresh AI text.

What this is not: proof that AI is "collapsing". The models were small, up to 973M parameters. The AI share is measured with Pangram's detector, and the work comes out of Pangram. AI text still helped when the goal was predicting AI text.

But the direction is hard to ignore. Every lab wants more data, and nearly a third of what's on the web is now machine output.

Human writing just became the scarce resource.

title: Inference traffic patterns for autonomous agent swarms look fundamentally different from traditional conversational chat.  Agents fire burst
text:
Inference traffic patterns for autonomous agent swarms look fundamentally different from traditional conversational chat.

Agents fire bursts of short execution steps that share massive, static context prefixes like codebase schemas and tool definitions.

If your inference gateway does not prioritize aggressive prefix caching and KV-cache reuse across concurrent agent calls, you pay a severe latency and cost penalty.

How is your infrastructure team optimizing inference caching for agentic tool-calling workflows?
